summary: O'Connor pressed ultimate-authorship objections and practical determinism; Carter answered with graded, attributable agency and nonreductive accounts of responsibility and moral meaning.

pro.text: you can do whatever you will you just can't will what you will
pro.context: O'Connor uses the distinction between acting on a desire and selecting that desire to challenge whether voluntary conduct supplies ultimate control.

con.text: the cause can be roughly designated as myself
con.context: Carter accepts that free conduct is caused, then relocates freedom in the difference between compulsion and action attributable to the person.

move-pro-01-control-dilemma.words: Free will appears to require authorship and a genuine ability to do otherwise, yet determined events inherit prior causes while random events provide no agent control.
move-pro-01-control-dilemma.critique: Strongest feature: The control dilemma establishes O'Connor's central route with a lucid contrast between events fixed by prior reasons and events occurring randomly without guidance from an agent. Principal limitation: Its conclusion relies on an approximately defined conception of authorship and does not establish why philosophically relevant freedom must include ultimate origination or categorical alternatives. Live burden: O'Connor must answer Carter's proposal that attributable, reasons-responsive voluntary conduct supplies meaningful control even when neither the agent nor the action is causally self-created. Locked score: The move belongs securely in the strong and competent band because it is foundational, coherent, and highly relevant, while its warrant and charity remain limited by the undefended standard of control itself and its broad scope claim throughout.

move-pro-03-causal-regress-of-desire.words: Any desire or mental choice is either uncontrolled randomness or the product of an antecedent causal chain, so neither alternative supplies ultimate control over wanting.
move-pro-03-causal-regress-of-desire.critique: Strongest feature: The desire regress applies O'Connor's causal dilemma directly to motivation, clearly showing why merely locating an action inside the mind does not terminate questions about control. Principal limitation: The categorical division treats causal dependence as sufficient to defeat every relevant form of agency, without considering how organized, reasons-responsive processes might constitute agent-level control. Live burden: O'Connor must justify moving from the unchosen history of a desire to the absence of attributable freedom, rather than only to the absence of ultimate self-creation. Locked score: The move fits the strong and competent band because its proposition is recoverable, central, and forcefully responsive to the debate's main issue, yet its universal scope, missing qualification, and compressed treatment of compatibilism materially restrict the inference advanced.

move-con-01-attributable-causation.words: Deterministic causation need not eliminate freedom because compelled conduct differs from voluntary conduct when the operative cause can appropriately be attributed to the acting person.
move-con-01-attributable-causation.critique: Strongest feature: Carter directly accepts causation while reframing freedom through the recognizable distinction between compelled behavior and voluntary action whose operative cause belongs to the acting person. Principal limitation: The phrase designating a cause as oneself remains schematic, leaving unclear which psychological organization, identification, or responsiveness conditions make attribution philosophically sufficient rather than merely conventional. Live burden: Carter must explain why personal attribution answers O'Connor's demand for control over antecedent wants, instead of changing the subject from ultimate authorship to ordinary voluntariness. Locked score: The move earns placement in the very strong band through exceptional responsiveness, clear burden contact, and a coherent compatibilist criterion, while its approximate account of self-causation and incomplete engagement with ultimate authorship prevent a fully decisive resolution here.

move-pro-04-unchosen-wants.words: Choices arise from force or from what an agent wants; force plainly defeats control, while acting from wants cannot supply ultimate control when those wants were not chosen.
move-pro-04-unchosen-wants.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor answers attributable causation directly by distinguishing the ability to act on a want from the deeper inability simply to select the want that motivates action. Principal limitation: The want-or-force dichotomy assumes without sufficient defense that freedom requires control over desire itself, overlooking compatibilist accounts grounded in reasons-responsive endorsement or ordinary voluntary capacities. Live burden: O'Connor must show why an agent cannot exercise meaningful control through unchosen but integrated motives, rather than merely establishing that nobody authors the entire history of wanting. Locked score: The move sits firmly in the strong and competent band because it sharply contacts Carter's sufficiency claim and advances the central route, although its universal scope, absent qualification, and limited treatment of graded agency constrain its warrant.

move-con-03-degrees-of-voluntariness.words: Freedom concerns context-sensitive degrees of voluntary control: a person may inhibit a sneeze but not an involuntary tic, even though neither underlying impulse was independently chosen.
move-con-03-degrees-of-voluntariness.critique: Strongest feature: Carter replaces the demand for choosing desires with a discriminating account of graded control, using inhibition of a sneeze and inability to stop a tic effectively. Principal limitation: These examples establish ordinary differences in voluntariness but do not themselves demonstrate that such local capacities answer O'Connor's distinct challenge concerning ultimate sourcehood and antecedent desires. Live burden: Carter must connect degrees of behavioral regulation to a principled criterion of freedom that explains why causal inheritance is irrelevant without merely relying on familiar usage. Locked score: The move belongs in the very strong band because it is precise, proportionate, charitable, and exceptionally responsive to both the unchosen-wants claim and causal regress, although the deeper metaphysical objection remains available after the practical reframe.

move-con-04-undeliberated-voluntary-acti.words: An action may count as voluntary and belong to an agent without being consciously manufactured through prior deliberation, because freedom admits degrees expressed through practical capacities.
move-con-04-undeliberated-voluntary-acti.critique: Strongest feature: Carter usefully separates voluntary ownership from conscious manufacture, thereby addressing the assumption that an action belongs to someone only when every motivating element was deliberately selected. Principal limitation: The selected evidence supports graded inhibition more explicitly than undeliberated ownership, so the distinctive inference depends partly on an idea developed more clearly elsewhere in the exchange. Live burden: Carter must specify how ordinary capacities make an undeliberated act attributable while distinguishing such action from compulsive, alienated, or otherwise uncontrolled behavior generated within the same person. Locked score: The move fits the strong and competent band because it contacts the decisive ownership issue and preserves the metaphysical distinction fairly, but partial proposition recovery and a compressed evidential basis keep it below Carter's strongest replies.

move-pro-07-consequentialist-responsibil.words: Abandoning ultimate desert leaves prevention, deterrence, and rehabilitation intact because incentives can alter the balance of desires governing conduct without requiring metaphysically self-created agency.
move-pro-07-consequentialist-responsibil.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor gives a concrete forward-looking account of responsibility, explaining how deterrent consequences can change behavior while remaining consistent with denial of ultimate moral desert. Principal limitation: The framework preserves prevention and rehabilitation but does not fully address Carter's claim that responsibility also contains interpersonal answerability, recognition, and ethical meanings beyond behavioral management. Live burden: O'Connor must show either that consequential practices can incorporate those relational dimensions or that invoking freedom adds no necessary ethical content to treating persons as answerable. Locked score: The move reaches the very strong band through clear reasoning, strong practical warrant, and a substantive answer to fears that determinism disables social response, while its relevance is subsidiary and its treatment of nonconsequential responsibility remains compressed rather than refuted.

move-con-07-interpersonal-responsibility.words: Responsibility includes an ethically important interpersonal practice of recognizing persons as answerable agents, while freedom operates through nuanced semantic and practical distinctions rather than an absolute metaphysical possession.
move-con-07-interpersonal-responsibility.critique: Strongest feature: Carter identifies a genuine omission in the consequentialist account by presenting responsibility as interpersonal recognition of persons, not merely an instrument for deterrence or behavioral management. Principal limitation: The ethical importance of that practice is asserted more strongly than defended, and its value does not establish that applying the label freedom is necessary to preserve it. Live burden: Carter must explain why answerability requires compatibilist freedom rather than a determinist practice that respects reasons, relationships, and consequences while rejecting ultimate desert. Locked score: The move fits the strong and competent band because it is highly responsive, charitable, and central to nonreductive personhood, yet elastic semantic language and limited warrant for indispensability prevent the reframe from decisively defeating O'Connor's practical position.

move-pro-02-substrate-neutral-dilemma.words: Moving agency into a soul, immaterial entity, or divine framework cannot escape the determined-or-undetermined dilemma, so changing the causal substrate does not create ultimate control.
move-pro-02-substrate-neutral-dilemma.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor consistently extends the determined-or-random dilemma across physical and immaterial substrates, closing an intuitive escape route without depending on a specifically neurological account of action. Principal limitation: Carter's compatibilism never relies on souls or uncaused entities, so this extension addresses a nearby metaphysical alternative rather than the attributable, graded, and interpersonal accounts actually advanced. Live burden: O'Connor must apply the substrate-neutral reasoning to Carter's organizational conception of agency and show why causally realized ownership cannot count as freedom on its own terms. Locked score: The move enters the strong and competent band because it is coherent, relevant to the central causal bridge, and epistemically qualified, but its relevant-nonanswer status and limited representational charity substantially reduce its effectiveness as a reply.

move-pro-08-determinist-compassion.words: Remembering that wrongdoers may not control the determining factors behind their conduct can encourage compassion, forgiveness, and understanding while leaving protective social responses available.
move-pro-08-determinist-compassion.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor presents compassion as a modest possible consequence of recognizing causal constraint, carefully avoiding the stronger claim that determinism automatically makes everyone kinder or more forgiving. Principal limitation: The practical suggestion is plausible but supported mainly by an illustrative psychological reflection, without evidence that determinist framing reliably improves compassion or avoids excusing harmful conduct. Live burden: O'Connor must explain how charitable understanding can coexist with victims' needs, protective boundaries, and differentiated responses to agents who display varying capacities for reflection and behavioral change. Locked score: The move fits the strong and competent band because its reasoning is coherent, explicitly conditional, and relevant to practical responsibility, while its subsidiary role, limited empirical warrant, and lack of direct engagement with Carter's interpersonal ethics restrain its reach.

move-con-08-ethical-tension.words: Ethical judgment should hold together the pictures of responsible choice and causal helplessness, preserving a plural understanding of persons instead of collapsing agency into either extreme.
move-con-08-ethical-tension.critique: Strongest feature: Carter offers a humane plural framework in which ethical judgment can retain both the image of a person choosing and awareness of powerful causal constraints. Principal limitation: The language of pictures and tension remains metaphorical, and the usefulness of multiple perspectives does not by itself establish the truth or necessity of compatibilist freedom. Live burden: Carter must supply a criterion for reconciling the pictures when they recommend conflicting judgments, while showing that O'Connor's determinism cannot preserve the same ethical plurality without freedom language. Locked score: The move belongs in the strong and competent band because it is coherent, proportionate, central to nonreductive personhood, and reasonably charitable, though its compressed metaphor leaves the inference from interpretive usefulness to agency incomplete and philosophically contestable.

move-pro-09-evolved-moral-desire.words: Moral motivation may arise through evolved emotional desires that compete with other motives and promote cooperation, giving stable societies a causal basis for inhibiting destructive conduct.
move-pro-09-evolved-moral-desire.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor supplies a positive causal account of moral motivation, connecting cooperative stability with inherited dispositions that compete against desires for violence or other destructive conduct. Principal limitation: The explanation shifts among genes, organisms, societies, intuitions, and desires without carefully separating biological selection, cultural transmission, psychological motivation, and normative justification. Live burden: O'Connor must clarify that an evolutionary genealogy explains why moral impulses occur without assuming it exhausts their meaning, authority, or susceptibility to rational evaluation. Locked score: The move qualifies for the strong and competent band because its hypothesis is coherent, relevant, and cautiously presented, but limited evidence, shifting explanatory levels, and no developed comparison with cultural or normative alternatives prevent the causal sketch from carrying broader reductionist implications.

move-con-09-normative-nonreduction.words: Explaining moral intuition through psychology or evolution does not eliminate its normative significance, because causal motivation and the richer meaning of moral judgment answer different questions.
move-con-09-normative-nonreduction.critique: Strongest feature: Carter precisely diagnoses a category problem, allowing psychological and evolutionary causes of motivation while denying that those causes exhaust the richer normative concept of moral intuition. Principal limitation: The reply defeats only an exhaustive or debunking interpretation, whereas O'Connor's stated causal account can survive if offered merely as an explanation of motivation rather than meaning. Live burden: Carter must specify the irreducibly normative features at issue and explain how they bear on freedom, instead of resting on the intuition that moral language is simply richer. Locked score: The move reaches the very strong band because it is direct, stable, calibrated, and charitable toward causal explanation while preserving a genuine conceptual distinction, though its relevance is subsidiary and its positive account of normativity remains brief.

move-pro-05-unchosen-source-regress.words: Choices reflect upbringing, genetics, circumstances, and dispositions that agents did not create, so tracing conduct backward never arrives at an ultimately self-created source of agency.
move-pro-05-unchosen-source-regress.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor concretizes the sourcehood regress through upbringing, parents, genetics, environment, and conformity, directly challenging any attempt to treat the present self as an unexplained causal endpoint. Principal limitation: The universal claim about human behavior exceeds the analogy and same-conditions counterfactual, while the regress establishes lack of ultimate origination more readily than lack of attributable agency. Live burden: O'Connor must explain why a causally formed person cannot nevertheless be the relevant source of action, and must address Carter's distinction between causal history and personal meaning. Locked score: The move remains in the mixed band because it is central and materially contacts attribution and graded control, but materially overstated force, missing qualification, incomplete responsiveness, and limited charity weaken an otherwise intelligible argument.

move-con-05-reflexive-first-person-persp.words: A self-aware person can react against a disclosed prediction, suggesting that first-person reflexivity complicates third-person prediction and resists treating agency as a fully static, externally described object.
move-con-05-reflexive-first-person-persp.critique: Strongest feature: Carter introduces a potentially important first-person complication by emphasizing that self-aware subjects can incorporate descriptions or predictions into the very conduct being described. Principal limitation: The selected passage recovers the existential perspective more clearly than the prediction-defeat mechanism, and reflexive resistance could itself remain causally determined by disclosed information. Live burden: Carter must distinguish epistemic difficulty in predicting a self-referential system from metaphysical freedom, then connect that distinction directly to O'Connor's regress through unchosen sources. Locked score: The move sits in the mixed band because its tentative framing and nonreductive theme are relevant and intellectually suggestive, but partial recoverability, weak contact with decisive targets, and limited evidence leave it a relevant nonanswer rather than a developed rebuttal.

move-con-02-mediopassive-agency.words: Some actions are simultaneously things a person does and things happening to that person, so genuine ownership need not require deliberate manufacture of every underlying thought or desire.
move-con-02-mediopassive-agency.critique: Strongest feature: Carter's mediopassive model offers a clear conceptual alternative to total manufacture, showing how an event may genuinely belong to someone while also occurring through unchosen processes. Principal limitation: The grammatical and marriage examples establish the category's intelligibility more readily than they show that ordinary voluntary actions generally possess the relevant ownership structure. Live burden: Carter must articulate conditions distinguishing mediopassive agency from events merely happening within a person, while acknowledging that attribution still may not satisfy ultimate-source demands. Locked score: The move belongs in the very strong band because it coherently contacts three decisive challenges, supplies a memorable practical model, and remains proportionate, though its generalization is compressed and it reframes rather than disproves O'Connor's separate conception of authorship.

move-pro-06-introspective-mechanism-gap.words: A person can intentionally move while lacking introspective access to how wanting or deciding produces bodily motion, as illustrated by the immediate instruction to move a finger.
move-pro-06-introspective-mechanism-gap.critique: Strongest feature: O'Connor uses an accessible bodily example to expose the striking gap between intentionally issuing a simple instruction and understanding the mechanism through which the movement follows. Principal limitation: Limited introspective access does not establish absence of agency, and the selected evidence only partly recovers the stronger proposition concerning a gap between wanting, deciding, and motion. Live burden: O'Connor must connect the epistemic observation to an eligible route requirement, explaining why ignorance of implementation bears on control rather than merely reflecting ordinary cognitive architecture. Locked score: The move remains in the mixed band because it is coherent, exploratory, and appropriately calibrated as a question, while exceptionally weak burden contact, partial evidential recovery, and no developed opposing alternative make it peripheral to the decisive exchange.

move-con-06-public-first-consciousness.words: Conscious thought may be socially and behaviorally constituted through feedback before private representation, so reductive inspection should not treat experience as a discrete, isolated internal object.
move-con-06-public-first-consciousness.critique: Strongest feature: Carter's pain example and feedback-loop account provide meaningful adjacent evidence for viewing consciousness as dynamically related to public behavior rather than as an isolated inner object. Principal limitation: Public and private shift between behavioral, epistemic, and constitutive meanings, while observable pain behavior may evidence experience without metaphysically constituting the experience itself. Live burden: Carter must distinguish evidence from constitution and directly explain how the public-first thesis answers either O'Connor's introspective mechanism gap or his causal regress through unchosen sources. Locked score: The move remains in the mixed band because it is coherent, relevant to dynamic consciousness, and conceptually suggestive, but unstable terms, underdefended breadth, and failure to contact both decisive targets prevent the reply from resolving the agency question.

strengths: The determined-or-random dilemma and its application to desires supplied a consistent central route focused on ultimate authorship rather than mere absence of external coercion.
The unchosen-wants reply directly challenged the sufficiency of attributable causation by separating acting according to a desire from selecting the desire that governs action.
The account of deterrence, prevention, and rehabilitation showed that rejecting ultimate desert need not eliminate practical responses to harmful conduct.
The compassion argument was carefully conditional, preserving protective practices while identifying a plausible ethical benefit of attending to causal constraint.

blunders.text: The source regress generalized from upbringing, genetics, and conformity to all human behavior without enough qualification, overstating what the examples established about attributable agency.

tags.label: Scope neglect
tags.context: The move did not proportion its conclusion to the limited conformity analogy and same-background counterfactual used as support.

blunders.text: The substrate-neutral dilemma pursued souls and immaterial causes even though Carter's compatibilist replies depended on attributable organization, graded control, and interpersonal practice.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: The move closed a nearby metaphysical escape route while leaving the opponent's actual substrate-neutral criteria substantially unanswered.

strengths: The attributable-causation reply accepted deterministic premises while clearly preserving the ordinary and philosophical distinction between compulsion and action arising from the person.
The graded-voluntariness examples supplied a concrete, context-sensitive alternative to requiring that agents independently choose every desire motivating their conduct.
The mediopassive account strengthened personal attribution by explaining how an action may belong to someone without having been deliberately manufactured in every respect.
The normative-nonreduction reply carefully allowed causal explanations of moral motivation while preserving a distinct question about moral meaning and authority.
The interpersonal-responsibility account identified ethical recognition and answerability as dimensions not exhausted by deterrence or behavioral management.

blunders.text: The reflexive first-person reply suggested that reacting against a prediction escapes reduction, but it did not show why that reaction could not itself be causally determined.

tags.label: Argument from ignorance
tags.context: Difficulty predicting a self-referential subject was treated as suggestive of freedom without positive support for a metaphysical escape from determination.

blunders.text: The public-first consciousness reply moved between behavioral evidence, social constitution, and private experience without stabilizing those distinct meanings or answering the mechanism challenge.

tags.label: Equivocation
tags.context: The terms public and private shifted across evidential, behavioral, and constitutive senses, making the conclusion appear broader than its example supported.

thesis.text: The strongest determinist conclusion is not that human deliberation is unreal, but that no agent ultimately deserves credit or blame for the causally inherited architecture through which deliberation operates.

novelty.explanation: This preserves practical and attributable agency while narrowing the denied freedom to ultimate authorship and desert.

premises.text: Whether an action is random or determined, its ultimate origin is not selected by the agent: randomness supplies no authorship, while determination traces the operative state to prior conditions.

novelty.explanation: This develops the causal dilemma while explicitly limiting its conclusion to ultimate origin.

premises.text: Reasons-responsive capacities can genuinely belong to a person and distinguish voluntary conduct from compulsion without making that person the creator of those capacities or their formative history.

novelty.explanation: This concedes the compatibilist distinction while showing that attribution and ultimate sourcehood remain separate questions.

premises.text: Because character, evaluative habits, opportunities, and capacities for self-correction arise through unchosen biological and social conditions, later reflection cannot retroactively create its own ultimate source.

novelty.explanation: This replaces the transcript's universal same-conditions claim with a narrower argument about retroactive self-creation.

premises.text: Forward-looking responsibility can assess capacities, request reasons, protect others, deter misconduct, and rehabilitate agents without adding the claim that anyone ultimately authored the basis of conduct.

novelty.explanation: This extends practical responsibility to include interpersonal answerability rather than reducing it to deterrence alone.

premises.text: Causal explanation and normative evaluation answer different questions, so acknowledging the evolved or social formation of moral motivation need not erase moral reasons or interpersonal meaning.

novelty.explanation: This accepts the nonreduction objection and prevents causal genealogy from becoming an unsupported normative debunking argument.

conclusion.text: Agents may therefore exercise meaningful local control and participate in moral practices, yet ultimate desert should be rejected because nobody created the complete causal basis from which that agency operates.

novelty.explanation: The conclusion narrows the determinist claim while integrating the strongest compatibilist insights about agency and responsibility.

newArguments.title: The constitutive-luck argument
newArguments.text: Suppose two people possess different capacities for impulse control, empathy, reflection, and responsiveness to reasons because of developmental conditions neither selected. Their actions may still be voluntary in Carter's sense, and institutions may properly respond differently to their present capacities. Yet the difference in ultimate desert cannot be grounded in self-creation, because the very mechanisms used to deliberate and reform are among the inherited conditions at issue. This separates legitimate capacity-sensitive responsibility from the stronger idea that agents fundamentally deserve their starting points or resulting character.

novelty.explanation: This is a new argument from unequal constitutive capacities, not a restatement of any transcript move.

newArguments.title: Recursive revision without ultimate authorship
newArguments.text: Self-modification does not end the sourcehood problem. A person can notice a motive, assess it, and cultivate a different habit, but the ability to notice, the standards used in assessment, and the persistence needed for revision all arise from the person's existing causal organization. Revision therefore supports real agency and justifies encouragement, education, and answerability; it does not establish ultimate authorship. This argument answers the concern that determinism makes reflection idle while preserving the narrower conclusion that even successful self-formation begins from resources the agent did not originally choose.

novelty.explanation: This extends the source regress into reflective self-change while preserving the practical reality of revision.

thesis.text: The strongest compatibilist thesis is that freedom is a graded capacity for actions to issue from the person's reasons-responsive organization without coercive or agency-undermining constraints, regardless of ultimate self-creation.

novelty.explanation: This replaces rough self-attribution with a more explicit reasons-responsive and constraint-sensitive criterion.

premises.text: A useful concept of freedom should distinguish conduct produced through the person's deliberative capacities from conduct imposed by threats, seizures, compulsions, manipulation, or incapacitating disorders.

novelty.explanation: This develops the transcript's compulsion distinction by naming several agency-undermining constraints.

premises.text: That distinction can be causal throughout: what matters is whether reasons can guide action through the person's evaluative organization, not whether the causal chain begins with an uncaused choice.

novelty.explanation: This directly answers the regress by specifying why causal inheritance does not eliminate agent-level guidance.

premises.text: Freedom admits degrees because people vary in information, inhibition, reflection, opportunities, and susceptibility to coercion; responsibility should track those capacities rather than functioning as an absolute status.

novelty.explanation: This generalizes graded voluntariness into a capacity-sensitive account of responsibility.

premises.text: An action can belong to a person without deliberate manufacture when it expresses stable commitments and remains answerable to reflection, correction, and interpersonal requests for reasons.

novelty.explanation: This supplies clearer ownership conditions for the transcript's undeliberated and mediopassive examples.

premises.text: Ultimate desert may be rejected while retaining answerability, because asking for reasons, expressing demands, and supporting reform are practices that engage persons as responsive participants.

novelty.explanation: This reconciles interpersonal responsibility with the determinist challenge to ultimate moral desert.

conclusion.text: Determination therefore does not eliminate freedom understood as graded, reasons-responsive, substantially uncoerced agency, although it should temper desert claims and make responsibility sensitive to actual capacities and circumstances.

novelty.explanation: The conclusion preserves compatibilist freedom while incorporating the strongest determinist lessons about luck and desert.

newArguments.title: The intervention-profile argument
newArguments.text: Two actions may have identical remote causal histories in form yet differ sharply in freedom because they respond differently to present interventions. One agent would revise after receiving accurate information, a reason, or an opportunity to pause; another cannot respond because of compulsion or coercion. This counterfactual profile identifies an empirically meaningful capacity without requiring ultimate self-creation. It also explains graded responsibility: the more reliably an agent can understand reasons, regulate conduct, and alter future behavior, the stronger the practical basis for treating the action as free and answerable.

novelty.explanation: This newly grounds compatibilist freedom in counterfactual responsiveness to present reasons and opportunities.

newArguments.title: Ownership through diachronic integration
newArguments.text: Personal ownership need not mean creating a desire from nothing. A motive belongs to an agent when it is integrated across time with memory, commitments, evaluative habits, and capacities for later endorsement or correction. Alien compulsions and manipulative interventions can fail this test even when they occur inside the same body. Diachronic integration therefore gives substance to Carter's rough designation of the cause as oneself and to mediopassive agency: an act can emerge through unchosen processes while remaining connected to the continuing person who can understand, assess, and revise it.

novelty.explanation: This extends personal attribution with a temporally integrated criterion for ownership and correction.
